newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Norilsk strike talk lifts nickel; sceptics remain.
newsitem.headline: Norilsk strike talk lifts nickel; sceptics remain.

text.p: A possible strike at Russia's huge Norilsk Nickel plant drew divided reactions from metal analysts on Wednesday, who weighed up the likelihood of disruptions at the key nickel exporter to western Europe.
Some said there was real concern among nickel consumers and traders over the security of Norilsk supplies, which was helping to boost world nickel prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME).
"I think there's a lot of nervousness about a strike at Norilsk," said Fidelis Madavo, nickel specialist at London-based CRU International.
But other industry sources said that talk of disruptions to output was a storm in a teacup.
"At the moment a lot of people in the market are discounting it," said Jim Lennon, analyst at Macquarie Equities in London.

Earlier on Wednesday a top union official at RAO Norilsky Nickel's flagship plant in the Arctic town of Norilsk said workers had a draft proposal calling for a strike on March 15 over wage and vacation arrears.
Madavo estimated Russian nickel exports accounted for 25-30 percent of Western European nickel demand in 1996.
Russian refined nickel output accounts for one-fifth of the world's total, and Norilsk accounts for 85 percent of all Russian nickel output.

"The earlier talk of wage arrears (at Norilsk) was largely discounted by the markets, because it is happening all over the Russian mining industry, but as soon as the word 'strike' is mentioned, it is a whole new ball-game," Madavo said.
Two-thirds of the world's nickel is used in manufacturing stainless items like construction goods and cutlery.

The Norilsk union official, Boris Degtyaryov, said the strike proposal still needed approval by the plant's United Trade Union committee. But he said workers were seriously considering laying down their tools.

A spokesman for Norilsk management, which owes 900 billion roubles ($160 million) in salary arrears and overdue holiday payments, tried to play down the talk of strikes, saying the company would do everything it could to avert such action.
Management and workers are due to meet on March 1 to try to thrash out a deal.

Analysts said some Russian nickel stocks were likely to have been built up at Norilsk's main export outlet, the port of Dudinka. Shipments are sharply curtailed during winter months as waterways to Europe freeze over.

"Ultimately, there will be some impact if the strike goes ahead," Lennon said. "But I suspect the company has some kind of stocks built up during the winter, so the earliest a strike could hit supply would be mid-year."
Nickel futures on the LME, the world's price-setter for industrial metals, can swing wildly on signs of supply disruptions at Norilsk.
Norilsk's flagship plant last year produced 100,000 tonnes of nickel out of the Norilsk group's total 177,185 tonnes. The vast majority of this is exported to the West.

The plant accounts for a major slice of the world nickel market. Madavo estimated Western world nickel output at around 700,000 tonnes in 1996 and former Eastern bloc output at 281,000 tonnes. Of the latter, Russia produced 210,000 tonnes, he said.
"Any strike at the plant will have a major impact," he said.

LME three-month nickel futures spiked on Wednesday, and floor traders attributed the rise to news of the strike proposal. At 1600 GMT, prices were quoted at around $8,040 a tonne, which was $300, or four percent, above the day's low.
Nickel futures prices have recovered strongly from a low of $6,365 hit in December last year.
But analysts said the longer term rally was triggered by strong physical demand and fund buying as well as concern over Norilsk supplies to anxious Western buyers.
"The most interesting thing for nickel is that demand seems so strong," Lennon said. "In the fourth quarter 1996, we saw the highest output of stainless steel in the Western world ever."
($ = 5676 Russian Roubles)
